title: Lower Doon zoning and citywide housing items
subtitle: Lodging house deferral, downtown vision, school site traffic safety, tower proposals, street names and grant consolidation.
overview: The Planning and Strategic Initiatives Committee had a long agenda on housing and development. Its main recommendation was for the Lower Doon land use study. The committee recommended adopting the official plan changes and a zoning by-law that uses a lower-density zone (RES-4) for most of the neighbourhood north of Conestoga College, after residents raised concerns about compatibility. The recommendation passed unanimously {{vote:m7}}, and the amendment behind it passed on a recorded vote {{vote:m8}}.

Several large items were deferred so staff could gather more information. These were the citywide lodging house rules, a two-tower proposal at Fischer-Hallman Road, a new Catholic school on Woolner Trail, and a 55-storey tower at 417 King Street West. Most go back to the November 6 Council meeting. The school item goes to December 11 or sooner.

The committee also recommended endorsing a new downtown vision and principles, consolidating environmental grant funding, naming several private streets, and an 11-storey mixed-use building at 2934 King Street East. All of these are recommendations that Council must still adopt or change.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended adopting the official plan amendment and a zoning by-law that rezones most of the neighbourhood to RES-4 rather than RES-5, with 400 Doon Valley Drive kept as RES-5.

The committee deferred the proposal to allow lodging houses everywhere residential uses are permitted to the November 6 Council meeting, so staff can get legal advice and information on regional garbage collection.
The committee recommended endorsing the downtown vision and its principles, and directed staff to build an action plan for downtown from them.
The committee deferred the Catholic school application to the December 11 Council meeting or sooner, while staff work with the Region on pedestrian safety and traffic calming on Fairway Road North.
The committee deferred the two-tower proposal to November 6 so staff can consult the applicant on alternative building height configurations.
The committee recommended approving the official plan and zoning changes for a mixed-use development with 77 residential units and commercial space.

The committee recommended moving the Community Environmental Improvement Grant funds to the Neighbourhood Development Office to combine with the LoveMyHood Matching Grant, and repealing the related policy.
The committee deferred the 55-storey proposal to November 6 so staff can work with NAV Canada on impacts to the airport runway approach.

debate: On Lower Doon, several residents said the RES-5 zone did not fit an older neighbourhood of mostly one- and one-and-a-half-storey homes. They objected to the 11 metre height limit and to the parking and larger buildings that RES-5 allows. Staff said RES-4 and RES-5 have the same height and storey limits and differ mainly in unit counts and building types, and that the height limit matches the rest of the city. Staff also said some properties already have RES-5-equivalent zoning, so lowering them would be a down-zoning.

Conestoga Students Inc. supported more housing near the college and asked for mixed-use zoning on the commercial lands south of Homer Watson Boulevard. A landowner's planner made a similar request. Staff agreed to report back on that option.

On lodging houses, supporters said they are an affordable housing type, that minimum separation distances have been criticized by the Ontario Human Rights Commission, and that legal status makes licensing and inspections possible. Councillors raised concerns about rent levels, overcrowding, licensing capacity and enforcement, and regional garbage collection. They also asked whether licensing should come back at the same time. Staff said licensing changes are expected early in 2024.

On the Woolner Trail school, delegates and councillors supported the school but worried about children crossing Fairway Road North and the nearby roundabout, school bus idling, parking on local streets, and effects on an adjacent heritage farm. The school board said it supports the proposed safety measures and accepted a deferral. Staff said the Region had agreed to review speed limits but had not committed to specific measures.

On Fischer-Hallman Road, councillors and staff discussed how the 14-storey tower would sit close to low-rise homes across Rockwood Road. The applicant said the design steps down from an already-approved 33-storey building, and staff agreed to explore a softer transition with the applicant.
